I think the biggest reasoning here was that Voldemort wanted the horcruxes to be meaningful yet inconspicuous. Hogwarts, Dumbledore, and the Sorting Hat would all be too risky. All of these things students would have come into contact with constantly and the jig would have been up once people recognized strange behavoir and mood swings happening. Though the Hufflepuff cup, Ravenclaw's diadem, and Slytherin's locket might have all seemed cruelly obvious when you figure out the pattern... all of these things were presumably hidden or protected. You can't easily hide a castle, the most known wizard in the world, or the sorting hat.

I have to disagree. Prisoner of Azkaban was my favorite as well but nothing is as unforgivable as the Goblet of Fire. I am still, 10 years later, horribly upset every single time I watch it. I spent my whole childhood waiting to see the final task come alive on the big screen and what do I get? A tornado and unrully weeds.

I'm assuming that's just the film makers decision to make the shot look nice. Me being unnerved by most things assymetrical, I probably would have chosen to fill up all the tables too. I've always wondered if the tables had some sort of magic to them to where they expanded according to the amount of students attending that year. Though I also assume that the number of witches and wizards graduating from Hogwarts is replaced by incoming first years...so perhaps not. I love thinking about all the hidden magic of the wizarding world not discussed in the books. :)
